target_columns.name: product_line
target_columns.transformation: Direct passthrough from policies, used as grouping key

target_columns.name: claim_month
target_columns.transformation: Truncate claim_date to first day of its month via DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(claim_date), MONTH(claim_date), 1)

target_columns.name: status_group
target_columns.transformation: CASE mapping: 'Approved'/'Paid' -> 'Settled'; 'Rejected' -> 'Declined'; any other value (including NULL) -> 'Pending'

target_columns.name: claim_count
target_columns.transformation: COUNT(*) of claim rows per (product_line, claim_month, status_group) group after inner join to policies

target_columns.name: total_claim_amount
target_columns.transformation: SUM(claim_amount) per group, rounded to 2 decimal places with ROUND

quirks: INNER JOIN on policy_id silently drops any claims whose policy_id has no matching row in policies -- these claims vanish from totals with no error, so the PySpark job must preserve inner-join semantics exactly rather than defaulting to a left join

Status regrouping is a closed three-way bucket: only 'Approved' and 'Paid' map to 'Settled' and only 'Rejected' maps to 'Declined'; every other value including NULL, empty string, or any unanticipated status code falls into 'Pending' -- do not treat NULL status as a separate/error case

DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(claim_date), MONTH(claim_date), 1) always emits day=1 regardless of claim_date's actual day, effectively a month-truncation; if claim_date is NULL this expression errors/propagates NULL in T-SQL (YEAR(NULL) is NULL, DATEFROMPARTS with NULL arg returns NULL) -- confirm whether claim_date can be NULL in source data and replicate T-SQL's NULL-propagation behavior rather than Spark's trunc() which may differ

ROUND(SUM(claim_amount), 2) uses T-SQL's round-half-away-from-zero on a float/decimal; Spark's round() uses round-half-up (HALF_UP) semantics which usually match but can diverge at exact .005 boundary cases depending on underlying decimal precision -- verify SUM(claim_amount) column type (float vs decimal) since T-SQL float rounding can introduce tiny representation differences before rounding

GROUP BY repeats the full CASE expression for status_group (not an alias) -- this is standard T-SQL requirement, not a quirk requiring special handling in Spark, but confirms the grouping key is the post-CASE value, not raw status

ORDER BY claim_month, product_line only affects presentation order of the output and has no bearing on aggregated values -- do not rely on row order for correctness checks during reconciliation, but do replicate it if downstream consumers expect sorted output

No explicit handling of duplicate/multiple policy rows per policy_id -- if policies.policy_id is not unique, the inner join would silently fan out claim rows and inflate claim_count/total_claim_amount; this baseline assumes policy_id is unique and that assumption must be validated against the synthetic data generator, not assumed true in general
